source.title: Snapshot Ensembles: Train 1, get M for free
source.authors: Gao Huang; Yi-Xuan Li; Geoff Pleiss; Zhuang Liu; J. Hopcroft; Kilian Q. Weinberger

record.tranche_reason: The paper tests snapshot ensembling and reports test error, but does not test the catalog claim about memorizing arbitrary labels, the listed factors affecting the training–test gap, or measured gap properties.
record.gate_note: The reported test-error comparisons concern snapshot ensembles, cyclic learning rates, and ensemble size. They do not measure the arbitrary-label memorization/generalization claim or its mapped versions. The discussion of flat minima and generalization cites Keskar et al.; it is not a result of this study.
record.test_reason: The dropout baselines test V6: Section 4.2 explicitly compares single classifiers with and without dropout, and Table 1 reports held-out errors. The record overlooks these results. Snapshot ensembling itself does not test a listed version.
record.authors_conclusion: The record accurately summarizes the main conclusion: cyclic learning-rate training yields accurate, diverse snapshots whose ensemble improves held-out performance at the training cost of one model. This concerns training cost; multiple snapshots are evaluated at test time.
record.recipe_differences: Snapshot ensembling with cyclic learning-rate schedules; the mapped versions concern memorization/generalization, architecture, optimizers, batch size, regularization, network size, sharpness, and memorized-example removal.
record.method_sensitivity: Test error varies with dataset, architecture, restart learning rate, number and length of cycles, training budget, ensemble size, and whether the schedule is cyclic.

fits_no_version.finding: Cyclic snapshot ensembles improve held-out performance at the training budget of one model, with performance depending on cycle count, restart learning rate, and ensemble size.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Averaging snapshots obtained with cyclic learning rates can improve image-classification accuracy without increasing the training budget.

fits_no_version.finding: Parameter interpolation and softmax-output correlations distinguish cyclic snapshots from non-cyclic snapshots. These do not measure magnitude-aware sharpness or its association with training–test gaps.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Cyclic learning-rate schedules produce accurate snapshots with more diverse predictions than late snapshots from a standard schedule.

record.problems: The study reports benchmark test-error comparisons for its ensemble method, but these do not address the catalog claim. Some supplementary comparisons are figure-only; no uncertainty estimates are stated.
record.rows_left_out: No results were extracted because none measure a mapped version of the claim.

untested.parts: Random-label memorization and natural-label versus random-label held-out accuracy.
Width beyond that required for zero training error.
Convolutional versus fully connected architectures and learned local connectivity.
Adaptive optimizers versus SGD under different tuning budgets.
Batch-size comparisons and changes that recover large-batch performance.

Very small training sets, dropout-rate sweeps establishing excessive-dropout underfitting, fully connected classifiers, and removing dropout and weight decay together. Only dropout probability 0.2 is tested.
Magnitude-aware perturbation tolerance, its correlation with generalization gaps, and comparisons with other generalization measures.
Removing memorized examples versus randomly selected examples.

record.verdict_notes: The empty extraction and assertion that no results address any version are incorrect. V6 concerns held-out error, so a measured training–test gap is unnecessary. DenseNet-40 SVHN's dropout error of 1.79 is explicitly imported from Huang et al.; its comparison with 1.77 should not be treated as this study's own dropout experiment. No uncertainty estimates establish the significance of the smaller differences.

versions.untested_parts: Random-label fitting and held-out performance on natural versus random labels.
Width beyond the interpolation threshold and its effect on test error.
Convolutional versus fully connected networks and the role of local connectivity.
Adaptive optimizers versus SGD, their tuning, and generalization differences.
Large versus small batches under fixed epoch budgets and recipe changes.
Dropout's effect on the training–test gap across regimes.
Magnitude-aware sharpness and other measures as predictors of the training–test gap.
Removing memorized examples and measuring the resulting test accuracy.
